extracted.intended_audience: graduate student instructors, new faculty, and course coordinators in college mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing instructor training meetings, administering end-of-semester grading, and conducting classroom visits for college mathematics courses. Includes grading formulas, workshop design steps, assessment advice, and visit program structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing grades: official reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: The only official reason for changing grades is to correct clerical errors, or to replace a grade of I or X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If students request grade changes for other reasons, respond that the only official reasons are clerical correction or replacement of I/X. Except for clerical corrections, discuss any potential change with a course director before making it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-semester retention of exams
rubrics_metrics.description: If students do not pick up their exams, the exams should be retained for one year after the date of the final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final grade component weights
rubrics_metrics.description: Official breakdown for the final grade: Exam 1 – 15%; Exam 2 – 20%; Final Exam – 25%; Homework – 25%; In Class Work and Quizzes – 15%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These percentages are used in computing weighted scores and final grades for the course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute weighted uniform exam score (W)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each student calculate W = 0.15 S1 + 0.2 S2 + 0.25 SF (S1,S2 = midterm scores, SF = final exam score).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each exam is out of 100 so W ranges between 0 and 60. The weighted uniform exam scores are used to determine uniform grades according to course-wide ranges provided after the exam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining homework grades by matching distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework policy: 15 assignments × 20 points = 300 total. Sum cumulative homework score per student and plot from 0 to 300; select ranges for A, B, etc., so the number of A grades (and B, etc.) approximately matches the number of A grades earned on the uniform exam distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example cutoff ranges suggested (e.g., A: ≥235 etc.). The intent is to align homework grade distribution with uniform exam grade distribution rather than fixed numeric cutoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining quiz grades by matching distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Quiz policy: 15 quizzes × 10 points = 150 total. Sum cumulative quiz score per student and plot from 0 to 150; select ranges for A, B, etc., so counts by letter grade approximate those from the uniform exam distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example cutoff ranges suggested (e.g., A: ≥120 etc.). Same distribution-matching rationale as for homework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute weighted total score (ST) for final grade
rubrics_metrics.description: Final weighted total ST = W + 15*(Q/150) + 25*(H/300), where W is weighted uniform exam score, Q is cumulative quiz total, and H is cumulative homework total.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formula converts Q (out of 150) and H (out of 300) into components weighted 15 and 25 respectively to combine with W (out of 60).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive final grade cutoffs from component distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculate lower bounds for letter grades by adding weighted contributions from each component distribution: e.g., lower bound for A = (lower bound A from uniform distribution out of 60) + 0.1*(lower bound A from quiz distribution) + 0.0833*(lower bound A from homework distribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous calculation applies for B, C, etc. This produces final grade ranges consistent with component distributions and the ST formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow a stepwise process for designing training meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the sequence: 1) Read the section to be covered. 2) Identify goals for the session. 3) Decide on a strategy to address each goal. 4) Begin time management. 5) Plan the student activities. 6) Write scripts for mini-lectures. 7) Make an assessment plan. 8) Put it all together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'Lesson Planning Worksheet' sequence is a recommended framework for planning interactive training sessions and can be abridged as instructors gain experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training session should meet a real participant need
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful training sessions have a real need among participants to have the training session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the workshop solves a concrete problem or fills a perceived need rather than being purely theoretical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance notice and clarity of meeting purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants should have advance warning of the meeting and understand what the meeting will be about before they attend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate objectives, agenda, and expectations ahead of time to increase engagement and preparedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep sessions focused with a small number of well-defined goals
rubrics_metrics.description: The session should have a relatively small number of well-defined goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, limited goals help participants know what they will gain and prevent unfocused coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: State goals as participant outcomes, not coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Goals should describe what participants will get out of the session, as opposed to merely delineating what issues will be 'covered'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame objectives in terms of learner benefits and behaviors (e.g., 'able to design a writing prompt') rather than topics listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide opportunities for active participant contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be opportunities for participants to actively participate in and contribute to the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include pair/small-group tasks, discussions, or hands-on activities to model interactive classroom practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting leaders must have concrete, meaningful content
rubrics_metrics.description: The meeting leaders actually have something concrete and meaningful to say about the issues raised during the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid abstract speculation; provide concrete strategies, examples, and actionable advice relevant to participants' classroom realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain structural flexibility to address emergent participant issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of the meeting should retain enough flexibility so that it is possible to address issues that participants raise within the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build optional time or flexible agenda items to handle unanticipated but important concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: End the meeting on time
rubrics_metrics.description: The meeting ends on time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage time deliberately; participants value timeliness particularly when they sacrifice personal/professional time to attend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design workshop goals for writing in mathematics (seven target outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshop goals include: (1) help participants recognize 'good' mathematical writing; (2) show how writing reveals student understanding; (3) demonstrate that correct symbol manipulation can mask conceptual problems; (4) provide ideas for including writing without major course overhaul; (5) clarify educational objectives of different writing assignments; (6) identify issues in assessing writing; (7) equip instructors with practical feedback strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these goals to shape activities and assessment in a two-hour writing workshop or longer series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt workshop content to participants' prior experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor emphasis depending on whether participants already use writing assignments: if experienced, focus on assessment and variety; if novices, emphasize rationale and types of assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make assumptions explicit and select activities that match participants' current needs and readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sample student work and peer discussion to elicit features of good writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin sessions by giving participants sample writing to comment on and rewrite; compile a list of 'Features of Good Writing' from their contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This activity builds confidence about subjectivity concerns and grounds standards in concrete examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use writing-to-reveal-understanding demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Show matched examples where symbolically correct work is paired with written explanations revealing misconceptions, to illustrate how writing uncovers student thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overlays/contrasts of 'symbols-only' versus 'symbols+explanation' to prompt discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer a menu of writing assignment types and small-group planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe kinds of assignments (autobiographies, EXPLAIN questions, journals, long-term projects) and have participants brainstorm how to include them in upcoming topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize making assignments clearly contribute to learning and feasible to grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing writing: use checklists to guide grading
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce options (e.g., Crannell’s checklist) and encourage instructors to develop checklists of criteria to mediate subjectivity and improve consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklists increase equity and time-efficiency; tailor criteria to learning objectives and student writing levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing writing: manage consistency and workload concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that grading writing may appear subjective and time-consuming; adopt strategies (checklists, limited assignment scope, rewrites) to reduce burden and improve fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about grading criteria and consider workload when assigning frequency and length of writing tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrites and resubmission policies: set expectations and watch for superficial fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: If using rewrites, make clear that substantial revision is expected; beware students who make only minor modifications to obtain full points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design prompts and feedback to require conceptual rather than cosmetic changes (e.g., require reflective note explaining revisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive feedback should uncover conceptual gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide feedback that detects vagueness, dangling pronouns, and passive voice used to 'cover up' lack of understanding; prompt direct statements and reformulation to reveal true conceptual grasp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain common student reading/response patterns to comments (e.g., treating comments as a story) and offer strategies to elicit substantial revision and deeper understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical planning tips: fit critical parts into allotted time
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure critical parts of the meeting can actually be completed in the available time to avoid overtime and participant frustration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize agenda items; be willing to postpone nonessential items if time runs short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical planning tips: include active tasks when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to include opportunities for participants to do something active when this is possible and appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active tasks model classroom techniques and increase retention and buy-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical planning tips: start with warm-up or easy items
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin meetings with a warm-up or easier items to engage early arrivals and focus attention for the important points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use early attention for difficult/high-value items when most participants are attentive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alternatives to lecturing to promote change
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatives include: pose a question for small-group discussion; have participants plan a lesson using a technique; use role-plays; convert lists into worksheets; invite experienced guest speakers; have participants research and present topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose alternatives that model active learning and are feasible for the training context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of class visits: observational visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational visits conducted by course coordinators early in the semester to give immediate support, diagnose serious problems, and observe teaching practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use early observational visits to provide focused feedback and to keep coordinators connected with classroom realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of class visits: student-feedback visits (mid-semester)
rubrics_metrics.description: Student mid-semester feedback visits (conducted by coordinators or via instructors collecting their own) provide facilitated student opinions at a time there is still opportunity for meaningful change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mid-semester timing ensures students have enough experience to give informed feedback while allowing time to act on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of class visits: peer visits (end third of semester)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer visits pair instructors to give and receive feedback; useful later in the semester when instructors have gained experience and can participate in assessment of teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer visits build instructor independence in collecting feedback and reflecting on practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals for instructors from class visits (multiple outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Class visits can: help instructors develop and articulate teaching goals; point out positives to reinforce; provide private space to voice concerns; identify areas needing improvement; expand teaching strategies; offer interaction with experienced instructors; encourage reflection and self-assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visits to support growth rather than punitive evaluation; give concrete actionable suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals for trainers from class visits
rubrics_metrics.description: Trainers use visits to look for teaching ideas to share, to observe how instructors implement program techniques, and to identify particularly strong instructors for peer visit roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visits inform improvements to the professional development program and help identify exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design a semester-long visit program with sequenced visit types
rubrics_metrics.description: One recommended structure: two weeks in — observational visits; midway — student mid-semester feedback; last third — peer visits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sequencing moves instructors from dependency on supervisory feedback to independent ability to collect and reflect on feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schedule visits to avoid disruptive periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid scheduling visits right before exams, immediately after exams, and close to lengthy vacations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visits are most valuable when actual teaching is observed and students are not distracted by unusual circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximize visit value by observing authentic teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Value of visits is maximized when visitors can observe actual teaching and students are not overly distracted by unusual circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose class sessions that represent normal instruction rather than special events or review days.
